docs.title: connectionforge
docs.text:
Manage a tenant's connections to external services in Go: provider definitions, connections, sealed credentials, grants and bindings, and a broker that hands out authenticated HTTP clients so callers never handle a raw secret.

Pre-release

connectionforge has not been externally audited. Version 0.1.0 supports static API-token connections. Read Security first.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: One model for every connection Provider, connection, credential, grant and binding, with a lifecycle that separates what was decided from what was observed. Owns the credential lifecycle, not the API clients Provider SDKs stay in their own modules and receive an authenticated *http.Client through their WithHTTPClient option. Secrets stay out of sight Secret redacts itself everywhere it can be printed, errors carry a status and a request ID but never a body, and only the broker and providers can read a value. Tested connections A credential is validated with its provider before it is stored, and again on demand. A permanent failure moves the connection to needs_attention. Ports and adapters Encryption, authorization, audit, leasing and deployment secrets are interfaces your application supplies. Restricted egress A provider's requests reach only the hosts its manifest names, over HTTPS, never a private address.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a provider API client. It does not wrap the GitHub, Cloudflare or Stripe APIs.
  • Not a cryptography library or a secret manager. Encryption and secret retrieval are ports; use a key-management library such as keyforge and a secret manager such as omnivault.
  • Not a workflow engine. A connection can be used by workflows; it is not one.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Getting started connects a service end to end in a few minutes.
  • The user guide explains connections, providers, how to integrate with a host application, storage and security.
  • The design documents hold the requirements, the technical design and the roadmap.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page connects a fictional service, verifies its token, and makes an authenticated request, using the in-memory store and a test cryptographer. A real deployment replaces those two with a SQL store and a key-management adapter; see Integrating with a host.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/plexusone/connectionforge@v0.1.0

Requires Go 1.26.

docs.title: 1. Describe the provider
docs.text:
A provider is a manifest (what a person must supply, which hosts a request may reach) and a verification request. For a service that issues a static API token, the apikey provider is configuration only:

import (
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/provider"
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/provider/apikey"
)

p, err := apikey.New(apikey.Config{
    Manifest: provider.Manifest{
        Key:         "example",
        DisplayName: "Example",
        BaseURLs:    []string{"https://api.example.com"},
        AuthMethods: []provider.AuthMethod{{
            Key:    "api_token",
            Fields: []provider.Field{{Name: "token", Label: "API token", Secret: true, Required: true}},
        }},
    },
    // GET /v1/me proves the token works and names the account.
    Verify: apikey.Request{Path: "/v1/me", AccountIDPath: "id", AccountLabelPath: "name"},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
providers := provider.NewRegistry()
if err := providers.Register(p); err != nil {
    return err
}

docs.title: 2. Compose the pieces
docs.text:
import (
    cf "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge"
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/broker"
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/cryptotest"
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/service"
    "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/store/memstore"
)

store := memstore.New()
b, err := broker.New(broker.Options{
    Store:      store,
    Crypto:     cryptotest.New(), // tests only: use a key-management adapter
    Providers:  providers,
    Authorizer: authorizer,  // yours: may this principal do this?
    Auditor:    auditor,     // yours: where events go
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
svc, err := service.New(service.Options{
    Store: store, Broker: b, Providers: providers, Authorizer: authorizer, Auditor: auditor,
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

Authorizer and Auditor are small interfaces; the host integration guide shows each.

docs.title: 3. Connect
docs.text:
owner := cf.OwnerID("org-1") // the tenant: opaque to the library
actor := cf.Principal{Kind: cf.PrincipalUser, ID: "alice"}

conn, err := svc.Create(ctx, service.CreateInput{
    Owner: owner, Actor: actor,
    Provider: "example", AuthMethod: "api_token",
    DisplayName: "Production",
    Fields:      map[string]cf.Secret{"token": cf.SecretString(tokenFromTheUser)},
})

Create calls the provider's verification endpoint first. If the provider rejects the token, nothing is stored and the error wraps connectionforge.ErrInvalidCredential. On success conn holds the discovered account (ExternalAccountID, ExternalLabel) and state connected. The token itself is sealed and stored separately and is never part of conn.

docs.title: 4. Use
docs.text:
hc, err := b.HTTPClient(ctx, owner, actor, conn.ID, cf.Use{
    Consumer: cf.Consumer{Kind: "application", ID: "dashboards"},
    Purpose:  "traffic",
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
resp, err := hc.Get("https://api.example.com/v1/zones")

hc adds the token to each request and can reach only api.example.com. Pass it to a provider SDK's WithHTTPClient option and the SDK never sees the token either.

docs.title: 5. Keep it healthy
docs.text:
conn, err = svc.Test(ctx, owner, actor, conn.ID)
// conn.State and conn.Health now reflect the provider's answer.

conn, err = svc.Disconnect(ctx, owner, actor, conn.ID)

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
connectionforge is a library. Your application, the host, supplies where data is stored, how credentials are encrypted, who is allowed to do what, and where audit events go. connectionforge supplies the model, the lifecycle, the provider contract, the broker and the operations.

your application
  ├── implements   Cryptographer, Authorizer, Auditor, Leaser, SecretSource
  ├── registers    providers (a manifest and a verification each)
  └── calls        service (create, test, list, ...) and broker (HTTP clients)

connectionforge
  ├── service   operations, authorized and audited
  ├── broker    the only path from a stored credential to a request
  └── stores    in memory, or SQLite and PostgreSQL through Ent

docs.text: You are Read Building an application that lets people connect services Connections and their lifecycle, then Using a connection Adding a service Writing a provider Wiring connectionforge into a platform Integrating with a host and Storage Reviewing the design Security and the design documents

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Owner The tenant a record belongs to, an opaque string such as an organization ID. Every store method is scoped by it Provider An adapter for one external service: a manifest, validation and request authentication Connection An owner's relationship with one account at a provider. It holds no secret Credential One sealed version of a connection's authorization material Principal Who or what acts: a user, a service or an agent Use Why a connection is being used: a consumer and a purpose Grant What a principal may do with a connection Binding A consumer that depends on a connection

docs.title: Connections and their lifecycle
docs.text: A connection is an owner's relationship with one account at a provider. It is a record with a name, the account the provider reported, the permissions the provider says it holds, a lifecycle state, and observed health. It holds no secret; its credential is sealed and stored separately.

docs.title: State and health
docs.text:
Two things are tracked separately because they answer different questions.

Answers Changes when State What was decided? Someone connects, disconnects or reconnects, or a check finds a permanent failure Health What was last observed? Every validation, including temporary failures

A connected connection can show a failed last check, for example because the provider was briefly unavailable. That does not make it unusable.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
State Meaning May be used pending Created, not yet validated No connected The provider accepted the credential at the last check Yes needs_attention A permanent failure: revoked upstream, expired, or a permission lost No, until reconnected disconnected A person disconnected it; credentials are destroyed No revoked Revoked at the provider; terminal No 
pending ──validated──► connected ──► disconnected
                          │  ▲            ▲
                 failure  ▼  │ success    │
                     needs_attention ─────┘
                          │
                          ▼
                       revoked

Every store enforces the transition table; a change it forbids returns ErrInvalidTransition.

docs.title: Health
docs.text: Field Meaning LastValidatedAt When the provider was last asked LastValidation ok, failed or unknown LastError A classified message with the status and the provider's request ID. Never a response body ConsecutiveFails Failed checks in a row; reset by a success

docs.title: Failures are classified
docs.text:
Provider answers Error Effect on a check 401, other 4xx ErrInvalidCredential Permanent: state becomes needs_attention 403 ErrInsufficientScope Permanent: state becomes needs_attention 429 ErrRateLimited Health only 5xx, network error, unparseable response ErrTransient Health only

connectionforge.Permanent(err) reports whether an error is one of the permanent kinds.

docs.title: The operations
docs.text:
All operations are on service.Service. Each checks authorization through your Authorizer and records an audit event.

Operation Requires What it does Create manage Checks the supplied fields against the manifest, validates with the provider, then stores the connection and its sealed credential. A rejected credential stores nothing Get view Returns one connection List view Returns the owner's connections the actor may view, optionally filtered by provider and state Rename manage Changes the display name Test use Validates again and updates health and, for a permanent failure or a recovery, state Disconnect disconnect Marks the connection disconnected and destroys its credentials. The record stays, so the audit trail and bindings keep their reference Reconnect manage Replaces the credential, keeping the connection and everything bound to it. See below Bindings view Lists what depends on the connection, so a person can see what a disconnect would stop Bind, Unbind use Records, or removes, that a consumer depends on the connection for a purpose

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
A token expires, is revoked, or is rotated. Reconnect puts the connection right without creating a new one, so the features bound to it keep working:

conn, err := svc.Reconnect(ctx, service.ReconnectInput{
    Owner: owner, Actor: actor, ID: conn.ID,
    Fields: map[string]cf.Secret{"token": cf.SecretString(newToken)},
})

The new credential is validated with the provider before anything is stored, so a rejected one changes nothing. It must belong to the same account as the connection (ErrAccountMismatch otherwise): connecting another account is a new connection, so a feature never silently reads someone else's data. On success the connection is connected again with fresh health, and its credential has a new version.

Reconnect also recovers a connection whose sealed credential can no longer be read, for example after a lost key ring: the new credential is sealed without opening the old one. A disconnected connection can be reconnected; a revoked one cannot.

docs.title: Test, in detail
docs.text:
Test does not return the validation failure as an error. A failed check is a normal outcome that is recorded; read it from the returned connection:

conn, err := svc.Test(ctx, owner, actor, id)
if err != nil {
    return err // not found, denied, or the connection cannot be tested
}
switch {
case conn.State == cf.StateNeedsAttention:
    // the person must reconnect
case conn.Health.LastValidation == cf.OutcomeFailed:
    // a temporary problem; try again later
}

A connection that is disconnected or revoked cannot be tested and returns ErrNotUsable.

docs.title: Errors a caller handles
docs.text:
Error Meaning ErrNotFound No such record for this owner. A record of another owner is also not found ErrDenied The Authorizer refused ErrNotUsable The connection's state does not allow it ErrAccountMismatch A reconnect's credential belongs to a different account ErrConflict Another writer changed it first; retry ErrInvalidTransition The lifecycle forbids the change ErrCredentialUnavailable The credential could not be read or decrypted. The connection is not used; there is no fallback service.ErrInvalidInput A field is missing, unknown, or the auth method does not exist service.ErrNotAudited The change was made, but its audit event could not be recorded

ErrNotAudited is special: the operation succeeded, and the returned connection is valid. Treat the gap in the audit trail as an incident rather than retrying the change.

docs.title: Integrating with a host
docs.text:
connectionforge imports no key manager, secret manager, authorization system or application framework. Your application, the host, supplies five small interfaces and a store. This page shows each.

Port You supply connectionforge uses it to Cryptographer Encryption under a managed key Seal and open credentials Authorizer Your authorization Decide whether a principal may view, use, manage, share or disconnect Auditor Your audit trail Record each operation and each refusal Leaser Short exclusive leases Make a refresh single-flight across processes (the SQL store provides one) SecretSource Your secret manager Read deployment secrets such as OAuth client secrets and app keys Store Persistence Hold connections, credentials, grants and bindings: Storage

docs.title: Cryptographer
docs.text:
type Cryptographer interface {
    Seal(ctx context.Context, purpose string, plaintext, aad []byte) ([]byte, error)
    Open(ctx context.Context, purpose string, ciphertext, aad []byte) ([]byte, error)
}

purpose is always connectionforge.CredentialPurpose (connectionforge.credential). aad binds the ciphertext to its owner, connection and credential version, so it cannot be moved to another record: an implementation must fail to open a ciphertext with different aad or a different purpose. Run cryptotest.Run against your implementation to check.

An adapter over keyforge:

type keyforgeCrypto struct{ c *keyforge.Client }

func (k keyforgeCrypto) Seal(ctx context.Context, purpose string, pt, aad []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    e, err := k.c.Encrypt(ctx, keyforge.Purpose(purpose), pt, aad)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return e.MarshalBinary()
}

func (k keyforgeCrypto) Open(ctx context.Context, purpose string, ct, aad []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    e, err := envelope.Parse(ct)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    pt, _, err := k.c.Decrypt(ctx, keyforge.Purpose(purpose), e, aad)
    return pt, err
}

Declare connectionforge.credential as a purpose when you open the key system. cryptotest.New() is an in-memory AES-256-GCM implementation for tests; do not use it in production, because its key lives only in memory.

docs.title: Authorizer
docs.text:
type Authorizer interface {
    Allowed(ctx context.Context, p Principal, a Action, c Connection) error
}

Return nil to allow, or an error wrapping connectionforge.ErrDenied to refuse. Any other error is reported as a failure, not a refusal, so a broken authorization backend is never mistaken for "no".

The actions are view, use, manage, share and disconnect. A natural mapping onto a resource-role ladder is: view to view, use to edit, and manage, share and disconnect to manage. Creating a connection is authorized as manage on the connection about to exist; its Owner is set and its Revision is zero, which lets you decide by organization role alone.

The principal's Kind is user, service or agent. For an agent acting on someone's behalf the broker records OnBehalfOf; your Authorizer receives only the principal, so decide there whether an agent needs its own grant.

docs.title: Auditor
docs.text:
type Auditor interface {
    Record(ctx context.Context, e Event) error
}

An event has a time, a type, the owner, the actor, the connection, the provider, success and a reason. It never carries a secret or a response body. Event types:

connection.created, connection.validated, connection.state_changed, connection.updated, connection.disconnected, connection.deleted, credential.replaced, credential.refreshed, credential.revoked, grant.changed and access.denied.

Return an error if you cannot record. The service reports it as ErrNotAudited after the change was made; it does not roll back.

docs.title: SecretSource
docs.text:
type SecretSource interface {
    Secret(ctx context.Context, ref string) (Secret, error)
}

For secrets that belong to the deployment rather than to a tenant. Per-tenant credentials never go through it: they are sealed and stored by connectionforge.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text:
Every record carries an Owner, an opaque string. Use your tenant identifier, for example an organization ID, and never a name or slug that can be released and reassigned. Every store method takes the owner and returns ErrNotFound for a record of another owner.

With PostgreSQL you can enforce this a second time in the database with row-level security. See Storage.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
store, err := sqlstore.New(db, sqlstore.Postgres, sqlstore.WithTxHook(setTenant))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := store.Migrate(ctx); err != nil {
    return err
}

b, err := broker.New(broker.Options{
    Store: store, Crypto: crypto, Providers: providers, Authorizer: authz, Auditor: audit,
    Egress: egress.Policy{}, // HTTPS to each provider's hosts only
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
svc, err := service.New(service.Options{
    Store: store, Broker: b, Providers: providers, Authorizer: authz, Auditor: audit,
})

SystemForge is an example of a host: its connections package composes these ports from its key manager, authorization, audit trail and row-level security, and serves the service as an HTTP API.

docs.title: Writing a provider
docs.text:
A provider is an adapter for one external service. It has three parts: a manifest that describes it as data, a validation that proves a credential works and names the account, and a way to authenticate a request.

type Provider interface {
    Manifest() Manifest
    Validate(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m Material) (Result, error)
    Authenticate(r *http.Request, m Material) error
}

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
The manifest is declarative so a user interface can render a connection form and an agent can read what a connection needs. It contains no code.

Field Meaning Key Identifies the provider, for example cloudflare DisplayName Shown to people BaseURLs The only origins a request for this provider may reach AuthMethods One or more ways to connect: Key, Fields, Scopes, AccountSelection, HelpURL HelpURL Where a person learns to create the credential

A field is an input: Name, Label, Secret, Required and Help. A scope names a permission the credential should hold, with a description and whether it is required, so an interface can tell a person which permissions to grant.

BaseURLs are part of the security model: they are the egress allow-list. Give a provider with regions or editions one provider per host, or a constructor option that sets the base URL. Never let a stored connection carry its own URL.

docs.title: A static-token service needs no code
docs.text:
For a service that issues an API key or token, configure the apikey provider:

p, err := apikey.New(apikey.Config{
    Manifest: provider.Manifest{
        Key: "cloudflare", DisplayName: "Cloudflare",
        BaseURLs: []string{"https://api.cloudflare.com"},
        HelpURL:  "https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/",
        AuthMethods: []provider.AuthMethod{{
            Key:    "api_token",
            Fields: []provider.Field{{Name: "token", Label: "API token", Secret: true, Required: true}},
            Scopes: []provider.Scope{{Name: "Zone:Read", Required: true}},
        }},
    },
    // Proves the token works.
    Verify: apikey.Request{Path: "/client/v4/user/tokens/verify"},
    // A second request discovers the account, when the first does not name it.
    Account: &apikey.Request{
        Path:             "/client/v4/accounts?per_page=50",
        AccountIDPath:    "result.0.id",
        AccountLabelPath: "result.0.name",
    },
})
Config field Default Meaning Method api_token The auth method this provider implements Field token The field that holds the token Header Authorization The request header that carries it Prefix Bearer for Authorization, else none Precedes the token in the header Verify required A GET that validates the token Account none A second GET that discovers the account

A Request has a Path and dot-separated paths into the JSON response, where a number indexes an array: AccountIDPath, AccountLabelPath, and ScopesPath for an array of strings.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
Implement Provider when a service needs more than a header token: a signed request, a two-step handshake, or a different verification.

func (p *myProvider) Validate(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m provider.Material) (provider.Result, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, p.base+"/me", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return provider.Result{}, err
    }
    if err := p.Authenticate(req, m); err != nil {
        return provider.Result{}, err
    }
    resp, err := hc.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return provider.Result{}, fmt.Errorf("%w: %w", cf.ErrTransient, err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if err := provider.Classify(p.Manifest().Key, resp); err != nil {
        return provider.Result{}, err
    }
    // decode resp.Body, return the account
}

Rules that keep a provider safe:

  • Use the client you are given. It is already restricted to the manifest's hosts. Never build your own for a request that carries a credential.
  • Classify with provider.Classify. It maps statuses to the typed errors the service understands and records the status and request ID, never a body.
  • Never put a body, a header or the token in an error. A provider may echo a credential in an error response.
  • Call Reveal only here. Secret.Reveal is for provider adapters and the broker. A test fails if it is called anywhere else in the module; clear the copy you take.
  • Do not make the account discovery depend on a human. If the credential names no account, leave AccountID empty and let the display name identify the connection.

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
reg := provider.NewRegistry()
if err := reg.Register(p); err != nil {
    return err // invalid manifest, or the key is already registered
}

reg.Manifests() returns every manifest ordered by key, which is what a connection form lists.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text: Run the provider against an httptest server that returns the service's documented response shape. Check the request path and header, the discovered account, and that a revoked token yields ErrInvalidCredential without the token in the error text. Use obviously fake tokens in fixtures.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Not externally audited

connectionforge has had internal review only. It handles credentials that can expose a customer's data, so read this page and the technical design before relying on it.

docs.title: What it protects
docs.text:
A connection is a credential for a customer's account at another service. The module is built so that:

  • the credential is encrypted at rest under a key your key manager holds, bound to its owner, connection and version;
  • a caller never receives the credential: the broker returns an authenticated HTTP client;
  • the credential cannot appear in a record, an event, an error or a log line through the module's own code;
  • a request carrying a credential can reach only the provider's hosts;
  • a record of another tenant is never visible, in code or, with row-level security, in the database.

docs.title: Defences
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Stolen database contents Credentials are ciphertext; additional data binds owner, connection and version, so a ciphertext cannot be moved Cross-tenant access The owner is in every store method; the conformance suite proves refusal; optional row-level security repeats it in the database A secret in a log, error or response Secret redacts in every format; provider errors carry a status and a request ID, never a body; a test confines Reveal to the broker and providers Server-side request forgery through a configurable endpoint Hosts come from the manifest; HTTPS only; no redirect to another host; private, loopback, link-local and shared addresses are refused after DNS resolution A lost update under concurrency Compare-and-swap on the connection revision and on the credential version A credential that cannot be read The connection is not used; there is no fallback An authorization backend outage mistaken for "no" An Authorizer error that is not ErrDenied is reported as a failure

docs.title: What you must do
docs.text:
• Supply a real Cryptographer. cryptotest.New() keeps its key in memory and exists for tests.
  • Use a stable, non-reusable owner. An organization ID, not a slug or a name that can be released and given to someone else.
  • Fail closed in the transaction hook when there is no tenant.
  • Keep the egress policy strict in production. AllowPrivate and AllowHTTP exist for tests against local fakes; leave them off.
  • Back up your key material with the database. Without the key, stored credentials cannot be read.
  • Ask providers for the narrowest read permissions their features need, in the manifest's scopes.
  • Treat ErrNotAudited as an incident. The change was made.

docs.title: Secrets in your own code
docs.text:
• Hold credentials as connectionforge.Secret from the moment you receive them, and never convert to string except at the last moment a provider needs it.
  • Do not log a request body from a provider call.
  • Do not put a credential in a URL, a query string or an error message.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Static API tokens only in v0.1.0. OAuth with refresh, GitHub App installations and credential replacement are planned.
  • A client holds the credential it was made with. A disconnect applies to the next client.
  • Grants and bindings are stored but not yet managed by the service; your Authorizer decides.
  • Rate-limit observation, DPoP and agent-delegated authorization are not implemented. The model leaves room for them: a connection is not synonymous with a stored secret.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Report a suspected vulnerability privately to the maintainers through the repository's security advisories rather than in a public issue.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
connectionforge has two stores that pass the same conformance suite.

Store Package Use In memory store/memstore Tests and examples; the reference for behaviour SQL sqlstore SQLite and PostgreSQL through Ent, on your own database

A store implements connectionforge.Store, which is ConnectionStore, CredentialStore, GrantStore and BindingStore. The SQL store and memstore also implement Leaser.

docs.title: The SQL store
docs.text:
import "github.com/plexusone/connectionforge/sqlstore"

store, err := sqlstore.New(db, sqlstore.Postgres,
    sqlstore.WithTxHook(func(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx) error {
        return setTenant(ctx, tx) // for example, SET LOCAL for row-level security
    }),
)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := store.Migrate(ctx); err != nil { // idempotent
    return err
}
tables := store.Tables() // for your tenancy policy
  • You own the database. New takes an open *sql.DB, and you close it. The package imports no database driver; use the one you already use.
  • The schema is the module's. Ent code lives in sqlstore/ent. You do not regenerate or merge it into your own Ent client; you share the database, not the code generation.
  • Tables are prefixed connectionforge_: connections, credentials, grants, bindings and leases.
  • Every owned table has owner_id (text), and every query filters on it.
  • Ciphertext is stored as bytes. No column holds plaintext.

docs.title: Migrate
docs.text: Migrate creates or updates the schema to match this version of the module. Run it with a role allowed to change the schema, and not through the transaction hook. A change that alters stored data is called out in the changelog.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite needs foreign keys on (Ent requires it to migrate) and either one open connection or immediate transactions, so that concurrent writers queue instead of failing:

db, err := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:cf.db?_txlock=immediate&_pragma=foreign_keys(1)&_pragma=busy_timeout(10000)")
db.SetMaxOpenConns(1)

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Races are decided by the database, not by locks in the process:

  • UpdateConnection is a conditional update on the connection's revision. The loser gets ErrConflict and retries (the service retries a few times).
  • SwapCredential installs version n+1 only if the active version is n; a unique index on (owner, connection, version) decides concurrent swaps.
  • A lease is a row with an expiry, taken by a conditional insert or update, so refresh can be single-flight across processes. Expiry uses the store's clock, so processes sharing a database should have synchronized clocks.

docs.title: Row-level security
docs.text:
On PostgreSQL, enable row-level security on the owned tables so the database refuses another tenant's rows even if a query forgot its filter. Key the policy on owner_id, and set the tenant for each transaction in the hook:

func setTenant(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx) error {
    tenant, ok := tenantFrom(ctx)
    if !ok {
        return errors.New("no tenant in context") // fail closed
    }
    // set_config(..., true) is SET LOCAL, scoped to this transaction.
    _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, "SELECT set_config('app.current_tenant', $1, true)", tenant)
    return err
}

ALTER TABLE connectionforge_connections ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE connectionforge_connections FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY connectionforge_connections_tenant ON connectionforge_connections
  USING (owner_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant', true))
  WITH CHECK (owner_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant', true));

Repeat for each table Tables() returns. The lease table has no owner and is not part of the policy.

Test as an ordinary role

Superusers and the table owner bypass row-level security. Test your policy with an application role that owns nothing, or it will appear to work.

docs.title: The in-memory store
docs.text: memstore.New() returns a store and leaser that live as long as the process. memstore.NewWithClock takes a clock so a test can advance lease expiry. Nothing is persisted.

docs.title: Testing your own store
docs.text:
store/storetest is the conformance suite. Call it with a constructor and it checks owner isolation on every method, compare-and-swap under concurrency, the transition table, cascade on delete, ordering and that returned records are copies:

func TestConformance(t *testing.T) {
    storetest.Run(t, func(t *testing.T) cf.Store { return newMyStore(t) })
    storetest.RunLeaser(t, func(t *testing.T) cf.Leaser { return newMyStore(t) })
}

docs.title: Using a connection
docs.text: The broker is the only path from a stored credential to an outgoing request. You ask it for an HTTP client for a connection; it checks that you may, unseals the credential, and returns a client that authenticates each request.

docs.title: Get a client
docs.text:
hc, err := b.HTTPClient(ctx, owner, principal, connectionID, cf.Use{
    Consumer: cf.Consumer{Kind: "application", ID: "dashboards"},
    Purpose:  "traffic",
})

The broker, in order:

  1. Loads the connection for the owner. Another owner's connection is not found.
  2. Asks the Authorizer whether the principal may use it, and records a refusal as an audit event.
  3. Requires the state to be connected; otherwise ErrNotUsable.
  4. Reads and decrypts the active credential. Any failure is ErrCredentialUnavailable.
  5. Returns a client restricted to the provider's hosts.

Use says why: a consumer (an application, workflow or agent) and a purpose. It is passed to your OnUse hook, if you set one, for counters. An agent acting for someone sets OnBehalfOf, which is recorded with any refusal.

docs.title: What the client does
docs.text:
• Adds the credential to a copy of each request. The request you built is not modified.
  • Reaches only the provider's hosts. A request for any other host fails with egress.ErrRefused, as does a redirect to another host, plain HTTP, and a name that resolves to a private, loopback or link-local address.
  • Holds the credential it was made with. A disconnect or a replaced credential applies to the next client, so make a client per unit of work rather than keeping one for the life of the process.

docs.title: Hand it to an SDK
docs.text:
Most provider SDKs accept an *http.Client. Give them the broker's, and they authenticate and stay inside the allowed hosts without ever seeing the token:

hc, err := b.HTTPClient(ctx, owner, principal, id, use)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
client, err := someprovider.NewClient(someprovider.WithHTTPClient(hc))

If an SDK insists on a token argument, pass any non-empty placeholder: the broker's transport replaces the Authorization header, or sets the header the provider's manifest names.

docs.title: Check before you rely on it
docs.text: A connection can stop working between requests. Call Test when a feature starts and on a schedule, and show the person Health.LastError when a check fails. For a feature that cannot proceed, return a message that tells the person to reconnect, not a raw error.

docs.title: Dependencies are visible
docs.text:
Record a binding when a feature starts depending on a connection, so a disconnect can show what would stop working:

err := svc.Bind(ctx, owner, actor, id,
    cf.Consumer{Kind: "application", ID: "dashboards"}, "traffic")

Bindings are idempotent, and deleting a connection removes them. Through the service, Bind and Unbind require use, so whoever may use a connection may say that a feature depends on it, and Bindings lists them for anyone who may view it. Show that list before a disconnect:

bs, err := svc.Bindings(ctx, owner, actor, id)
// "Disconnecting stops: portfolio.site impactchiefs.com (traffic)"

A reconnect leaves bindings untouched.

docs.title: v0.1.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-10-13

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Connections without handing out secrets. A broker returns an authenticated *http.Client, which provider SDKs accept through their WithHTTPClient option, so a caller uses a connection without ever holding its credential.
  • Secrets cannot leak by construction. Secret prints as [redacted] in every format verb, in JSON, in text and in slog. Errors carry a status and the provider's request ID but never a response body, and a test confines Reveal to the broker and the providers.
  • Ports and adapters. Encryption, authorization, audit, leasing and deployment secrets are interfaces the host supplies. The module imports no key manager, secret manager or application framework.
  • A SQL store a host composes. An Ent-backed store for SQLite and PostgreSQL runs on the host's own database, with owner_id on every owned table and a per-transaction hook for row-level security.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: connectionforge v0.1.0 has not been externally audited. It supports static API-token connections. GitHub App installations, OAuth with refresh, credential replacement, scheduled validation and an HTTP API follow in later releases; the roadmap lists them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: connectionforge manages a tenant's connections to external services: the provider, the connection, its sealed credential, who may use it and what depends on it. It owns the credential lifecycle, not the provider's API client. The design is in the PRD and TRD.

docs.title: Model and lifecycle
docs.text:
Record Holds Connection Provider, auth method, display name, discovered account, scopes, state and health. No secret Credential One sealed version of the authorization material, with its expiry Grant What a principal may do with a connection: view, use, manage, share, disconnect Binding A consumer that depends on a connection, and why

State is what was decided (pending, connected, needs_attention, disconnected, revoked); health is what was last observed. A transient failure changes health and never state, and a transition table is enforced by every store.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• Secret copies on construction and on Reveal, and can be cleared.
  • Credentials are sealed with additional data that binds the owner, the connection and the credential version, so a ciphertext cannot be moved to another record.
  • A credential that cannot be read or decrypted makes the connection unusable. There is no fallback.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
• A provider is a declarative Manifest (fields, scopes, base URLs, help) plus validation and request authentication.
  • provider/apikey covers services that issue a static key or token: where the token goes, which endpoint verifies it, and where the account is in the response.
  • Classify maps HTTP refusals to typed errors: an invalid credential, an insufficient scope, rate limiting or a transient failure.

docs.title: Egress
docs.text: The HTTP client the broker hands out reaches only the hosts in the provider's manifest, over HTTPS. It refuses a redirect to another host and refuses private, loopback, link-local and shared addresses after DNS resolution, so a rebinding name cannot reach them.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Operation Behaviour Create Validates with the provider and stores nothing if it is rejected Get, List Return what the actor may view Rename Changes the display name Test Validates again. A permanent failure moves the connection to needs_attention; success moves it back; a transient failure changes only health Disconnect Destroys the credentials and keeps the record for the audit trail

Each operation is authorized through the host's Authorizer and audited. A change whose audit event could not be recorded returns ErrNotAudited: the change was made, and the gap is reported rather than hidden.

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
Store Use store/memstore Tests and examples; the reference for behaviour sqlstore SQLite and PostgreSQL through Ent, on the host's database

Both pass the same conformance suite, which covers owner isolation, compare-and-swap under concurrency, the transition table, cascade on delete and leases. The PostgreSQL run is opt-in with CONNECTIONFORGE_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/plexusone/connectionforge@v0.1.0

Requires Go 1.26.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
p, err := apikey.New(apikey.Config{
    Manifest: provider.Manifest{
        Key: "example", DisplayName: "Example", BaseURLs: []string{"https://api.example.com"},
        AuthMethods: []provider.AuthMethod{{
            Key:    "api_token",
            Fields: []provider.Field{{Name: "token", Label: "API token", Secret: true, Required: true}},
        }},
    },
    Verify: apikey.Request{Path: "/v1/me", AccountIDPath: "id", AccountLabelPath: "name"},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
providers := provider.NewRegistry()
if err := providers.Register(p); err != nil {
    return err
}

store := memstore.New() // or sqlstore.New(db, sqlstore.Postgres), then Migrate
b, err := broker.New(broker.Options{
    Store: store, Crypto: crypto, Providers: providers, Authorizer: authz, Auditor: audit,
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
svc, err := service.New(service.Options{
    Store: store, Broker: b, Providers: providers, Authorizer: authz, Auditor: audit,
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

conn, err := svc.Create(ctx, service.CreateInput{
    Owner: owner, Actor: actor, Provider: "example", AuthMethod: "api_token",
    Fields: map[string]connectionforge.Secret{"token": connectionforge.SecretString(token)},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
hc, err := b.HTTPClient(ctx, owner, actor, conn.ID, connectionforge.Use{
    Consumer: connectionforge.Consumer{Kind: "application", ID: "dashboards"}, Purpose: "traffic",
})
// hc authenticates each request; pass it to a provider SDK's WithHTTPClient.

crypto, authz and audit are the host's implementations of Cryptographer, Authorizer and Auditor. cryptotest.New() is an in-memory Cryptographer for tests.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Static API tokens only. GitHub App installations, OAuth with PKCE and single-flight refresh, and credential replacement are not in this release.
  • No scheduled validation. A connection is tested when Test is called.
  • No HTTP API or command line. A host exposes the service itself.
  • Grants and bindings are stored, not yet managed by the service. A host authorizes through its Authorizer.
  • A client holds the credential it was made with. A disconnect or a replaced credential applies to the next client, so make one per unit of work.
  • SQLite needs foreign keys on and one connection or immediate transactions so that concurrent writers queue instead of failing.
  • CI runs the SQLite conformance suite; the PostgreSQL suite is opt-in.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Module Use entgo.io/ent The SQL store

The module imports no database driver; the host chooses one. pgx and modernc.org/sqlite appear in go.mod only for the store tests.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: A user guide covers connections and their lifecycle, using a connection, writing a provider, integrating with a host, storage and security, starting from Getting started.

docs.title: v0.2.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-10-13

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Reconnect. service.Reconnect replaces a connection's credential without creating a new connection, so the features bound to it keep working.
  • Bindings through the service. Bindings lists what depends on a connection, and Bind and Unbind record it, so a disconnect can show what it would stop.
  • No breaking changes.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
A token expires, is revoked or is rotated. Reconnect takes the new credential, validates it with the provider before storing anything, and writes it as the next version:

conn, err := svc.Reconnect(ctx, service.ReconnectInput{
    Owner: owner, Actor: actor, ID: id,
    Fields: map[string]connectionforge.Secret{"token": connectionforge.SecretString(newToken)},
})
  • A credential the provider rejects changes nothing.
  • A credential for a different account is refused with ErrAccountMismatch. Connecting another account is a new connection, so a feature never silently reads someone else's data.
  • On success the connection is connected with fresh health, and bindings are untouched.
  • It recovers a connection whose sealed credential can no longer be read, such as after a lost key ring, because the new credential is sealed without opening the old one.
  • A disconnected connection can be reconnected; a revoked one cannot.
  • It requires manage, and records a credential.replaced event.

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
Operation Requires Behaviour Bindings view Lists what depends on the connection Bind use Records that a consumer depends on it for a purpose; idempotent Unbind use Removes a binding; not an error when none exists

Each change records a binding.changed event. Grants stay with the host's authorization.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go get github.com/plexusone/connectionforge@v0.2.0

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• A disconnect does not require acknowledging bindings. The list is available; requiring it is planned (RMI-CONNECTIONFORGE-018).
  • Everything in the v0.1.0 limitations still applies: static API tokens only, no scheduled validation, no HTTP API of its own.

docs.title: connectionforge: Plan
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-CONNECTIONFORGE-001 Repository: github.com/plexusone/connectionforge

Implements the PRD and TRD. The roadmap holds the work items and their status.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• Model and ports first. The data model, the lifecycle and the port interfaces are the parts that stored data and hosts depend on, so they are specified and given in-memory implementations and conformance suites before any provider or HTTP surface exists.
  • Secrets are a type, not a convention. The redacting secret type and the rule that the broker never returns one are built before the first provider.
  • Two reference providers that disagree. A static API-token provider and GitHub App exercise very different credential models and expose abstraction problems early. OAuth refresh follows once those are stable.
  • Library before service. The broker, validation and refresh are complete and tested with in-memory ports before handlers or a CLI exist.
  • Public-ready from the first commit. No host-specific facts, no customer references and no secrets in fixtures.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase Theme Outcome 1 Model, ports and secrets The types, lifecycle, ports, redacting secret type and in-memory stores with conformance suites 2 Static credentials and the broker An API-token provider validated end to end, with the authenticated-client broker and audit 3 GitHub App and OAuth Installation tokens, authorization code with PKCE, single-flight refresh 4 Operations Scheduled validation, health, rotation and replacement, bindings, grants and egress policy 5 Hardening and v0.1.0 HTTP API, CLI, documentation, threat model, review and release

docs.title: Dependencies and sequencing
docs.text:
• Phase 2's broker depends on the Cryptographer and CredentialStore ports fixed in phase 1.
  • Phase 3's refresh depends on the store's compare-and-swap credential update and the lease port from phase 1.
  • Phase 4's egress policy is applied by the broker, so it follows phase 2.
  • The release waits for a security review of the broker and refresh paths.

docs.title: Integration with a host
docs.text: connectionforge owns its domain, including its schema. A host application (for example a platform that already owns tenancy, authorization and storage) opens sqlstore on its own database, runs its migration, applies its tenancy policy to the tables it reports, supplies the remaining ports and mounts the optional HTTP package. The host's key-management library implements Cryptographer and its authorization implements Authorizer; those adapters live in the host.

docs.title: connectionforge: Product Requirements
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-CONNECTIONFORGE-001 Repository: github.com/plexusone/connectionforge

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Applications that integrate with third-party services (a code host, a CDN, an analytics product, a payment processor) each end up with a private, ad hoc way to hold the customer's credentials for that service. The same gaps recur:

  • Credentials are scattered. An API token in one table, an OAuth refresh token in another, a GitHub App key in an environment variable. There is no single inventory of which tenant has connected what.
  • Nobody knows whether a connection still works. A token is revoked or expires, and the first sign is a failed sync inside a feature.
  • OAuth refresh is easy to get subtly wrong. Two workers refresh the same token at once, the rotated refresh token is lost, and the customer has to reconnect.
  • Secrets leak through convenience. Raw tokens reach logs, API responses and browser code because the simplest way to use a credential is to hand it to the caller.
  • Every provider is a special case. GitHub Apps mint short-lived installation tokens from a private key; Cloudflare uses scoped API tokens; Stripe uses restricted keys or Connect. Each new provider re-solves validation, account discovery and revocation.

Hosted automation products solve this with a connection framework: a connection is an authorized account that is reusable, tested and labelled. There is no equivalent library for Go applications that is multi-tenant, encrypts credentials under a managed key, and is ready for agent-delegated authorization.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One model for every external connection: provider, connection, credential, grant, binding, with a single lifecycle.
  2. Own the credential lifecycle, not the API clients. Provider SDKs stay in their own modules; connectionforge supplies an authenticated transport, validation and status.
  3. Secrets stay server-side and out of normal paths. Callers receive metadata and an authenticated HTTP client, not raw tokens; secrets are redacted in logs, errors and JSON by construction.
  4. Correct refresh and rotation. Refresh is single-flight and persists a rotated refresh token atomically; replacing a static credential is a separate, audited operation.
  5. Tested connections. Every connection can be validated on demand and on a schedule, with account discovery and a human-readable account label.
  6. Ports and adapters. Storage, encryption, authorization, audit and egress policy are interfaces supplied by the host; the library imports no host framework.
  7. Declarative provider manifests. A provider states its authentication methods, fields, scopes and validation operation as data, so a UI or an agent can render and repair a connection without provider-specific code.
  8. Room for delegated authorization. A connection is not synonymous with a stored secret, so workload identity and agent-delegated grants can be added without changing the model.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Provider API clients. connectionforge does not wrap the GitHub, Cloudflare or Stripe APIs.
  • Cryptography. Encryption is a port; a key-management library implements it.
  • A secret manager. Retrieving bootstrap secrets (client secrets, an app private key) is the host's job, through a port.
  • A workflow or automation engine. A connection can be used by workflows; it is not one.
  • Authenticating or authorizing the host's users. The host supplies an authorizer and a tenant scope.
  • Shipping a UI in the core module. A UI kit built on the provider manifests is a separate, later module.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: User Needs Application developer Ask for an authenticated HTTP client for a tenant's connection; never handle a raw token Tenant administrator Connect, test, rename, reconnect, replace and revoke connections; see what depends on one Operator See which connections are failing or expiring; know that refresh and rotation are safe under concurrency Provider author Describe a provider and its validation once, with conformance tests, and have it work for every host Security reviewer Read a stated threat model and an audit trail that never contains a secret Platform integrator Plug in storage, encryption, authorization, audit and egress policy

docs.title: Functional
docs.text: ID Requirement FR1 A registry of provider definitions, each with a manifest: authentication methods, credential fields (marked secret or not), scopes, account-selection needs, validation operation FR2 Tenant-owned connections with a lifecycle state, a display name, an external account identifier and label, granted scopes and observed health, kept distinct FR3 Versioned, encrypted credentials separate from the connection record; the credential store never holds plaintext FR4 Static credentials: API keys and tokens, with validation and account discovery on create FR5 OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE, state and a validated return destination, following the current OAuth security best practice FR6 Automatic access-token refresh, single-flight per credential, persisting a rotated refresh token atomically, with classification of permanent versus transient failure FR7 GitHub App installations as a first-class method: installation tokens minted from the app key and cached until near expiry FR8 Connection testing on demand and on a schedule, producing a validation result and updating observed health without changing lifecycle state FR9 Reconnect, replace credential, rotate, disconnect and revoke, each audited; revocation calls the provider where it supports it FR10 A credential broker: HTTPClient and Token-less access that injects authorization per request, so a caller never receives the secret FR11 Grants: which principals (users, services, agents) may use, manage, share or disconnect a connection, enforced through a host Authorizer FR12 Bindings: which consumers (application, workflow, agent) use a connection, so disconnecting can report what would stop working FR13 Multiple connections per provider per tenant, and multiple credentials per connection during replacement FR14 Audit events for create, validate, use (sampled or counted), refresh, replace, revoke and administrative access, with no secret values FR15 Egress policy: provider endpoints come from the manifest, redirects are restricted, and private and link-local destinations are refused FR16 Conformance suites for the stores, the cryptographer port and providers, with recorded fixtures for provider adapters FR17 Rate-limit observation from provider responses, surfaced as health (later) FR18 Deployment secrets (OAuth client secrets, app keys) read through a host SecretSource port, never stored with per-owner credentials

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text: ID Requirement NFR1 A secret value has a type that redacts itself in String, GoString, MarshalJSON, MarshalText and slog; it is never an error message NFR2 Fail closed: if decryption, authorization or validation cannot complete, the connection is not used NFR3 Tenant isolation is part of every store method signature; a store conformance test proves cross-tenant reads and writes fail NFR4 Library-first: HTTP handlers and a CLI are thin adapters over the library NFR5 No import of any host framework, and no import of a key-management or secret-manager module in the core NFR6 Public-ready repository and history from the first commit NFR7 Ships an Ent-backed store for SQLite and PostgreSQL that a host composes on its own database, applying its own tenancy policy; a host may still supply its own store NFR8 Context-aware, cancellable operations; no goroutines that outlive the caller's context except a documented, stoppable scheduler

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
1. A host can store a Cloudflare-style API token, see it validated with a discovered account label, and obtain an authenticated *http.Client for it without the token appearing in any API response, log or error.
  2. Two processes refreshing the same OAuth connection at once result in one token exchange, and the rotated refresh token is not lost.
  3. A GitHub App connection produces installation tokens, caches them, and renews them before expiry without a stored long-lived token.
  4. Disconnecting a connection reports the bindings that depend on it before it acts, and the audit trail records who did it.
  5. A cross-tenant read, write or use is refused by every store implementation.
  6. A new provider can be added by describing a manifest and implementing the validation, without changing the core.

docs.title: Out of scope for v0.1.0
docs.text: The UI kit, rate-limit tracking, DPoP and mutual TLS, agent-delegated authorization and any provider beyond the two reference implementations (an API-token provider and GitHub App). The model is designed so each fits without changing stored data.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether the HTTP handlers live in this module or in the host. The default is a small connectionforge/httpapi package that a host may mount or ignore.
  • Whether usage events are recorded individually or as counters per connection per period.

docs.title: connectionforge: Technical Requirements
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-CONNECTIONFORGE-001 Repository: github.com/plexusone/connectionforge

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Provider A definition of an external service: its manifest and its adapter (validate, discover, refresh, revoke, authenticate a request) Connection A tenant-owned relationship with one account at a provider. Carries lifecycle state, observed health and metadata. Holds no secret Credential Encrypted authorization material for a connection, versioned. Only the credential store and the broker ever see ciphertext; only the broker sees plaintext Grant Who or what may use, manage, share or disconnect a connection Binding A consumer (application, workflow, agent) that depends on a connection Broker The only path from a connection to an authenticated request Owner The opaque tenant scope under which every record lives

A connection is not a stored secret. Its credential is one of the ways authorization is obtained, and the broker hides which.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
connectionforge is a library of ports and a core that composes them. It imports the Go standard library, golang.org/x/oauth2 and nothing from any host. The host is the composition root.

host application
  ├── implements Ports: stores, Cryptographer, Authorizer, Auditor, Leaser, Egress
  ├── registers Providers (adapters, each with a Manifest)
  └── mounts httpapi (optional) or calls the Service directly

connectionforge
  ├── Service   create, test, reconnect, replace, revoke, list
  ├── Broker    authenticated clients for a connection
  └── Refresher single-flight token refresh

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Responsibility Imports connectionforge (root) Types, errors, Secret, ports, lifecycle states stdlib provider Provider, capability interfaces, Manifest, registry root provider/apikey Reference static-credential provider driven by a manifest root, provider provider/githubapp GitHub App installations root, provider oauth Authorization code with PKCE, state, refresh root, x/oauth2 broker Authenticated http.Client and transports, token cache root, provider service Application operations over the ports root, provider, broker store/memstore In-memory stores for tests and examples root store/storetest Store conformance suite root sqlstore Ent-backed stores and leaser for SQLite and PostgreSQL, with migration root, Ent, drivers sqlstore/ent The Ent schema and generated code Ent egress Destination policy and an HTTP client factory stdlib httpapi Handlers over service, mounted by the host service cmd/connectionforge Thin CLI over service service

connectionforge owns its domain, including its database schema. The host composes it: it opens sqlstore on its own database, runs its migration, and applies its tenancy policy (for example row-level security) to the tables sqlstore reports. Ent and the database drivers are imported by sqlstore only, so a host that brings its own store does not pull them in.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
type Connection struct {
    ID                string
    Owner             OwnerID           // tenant scope; opaque to the library
    Provider          string            // provider key, e.g. "cloudflare"
    AuthMethod        string            // from the manifest: "api_token", "github_app", "oauth2"
    DisplayName       string            // human label, editable
    ExternalAccountID string            // discovered
    ExternalLabel     string            // discovered, shown to humans
    Scopes            []string          // granted, as reported by the provider
    State             State
    Health            Health            // observed, separate from State
    Metadata          map[string]string // non-secret provider settings
    CreatedBy         Principal
    CreatedAt, UpdatedAt time.Time
    Revision          uint64            // increases on every update; drives compare-and-swap
}

docs.title: Lifecycle state and observed health
docs.text:
State is what was decided; health is what was observed. A connected connection can have a failed last validation.

pending ──authorize/validate──► connected ──► disconnected
                                   │  ▲            ▲
                          failure  ▼  │ reconnect  │
                              needs_attention ─────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
                                revoked
State Meaning pending Created, not yet authorized or validated connected Credential accepted by the provider at last check needs_attention A permanent failure: revoked upstream, expired, scope lost. The broker refuses use disconnected Disconnected by a person; credentials destroyed revoked Revoked at the provider by connectionforge; terminal

Transient failures (network, rate limit, provider outage) change Health, never State. The transition table lives in code, is the single source for the documentation and is enforced by every store, which updates a connection only by compare-and-swap on its revision.

type Health struct {
    LastValidatedAt  time.Time
    LastValidation   Outcome   // ok, failed, unknown
    LastError        string    // classified, never containing a secret
    ConsecutiveFails int
}

Rate-limit observations join Health when rate-limit tracking is added.

docs.title: Credential
docs.text:
type Credential struct {
    Owner        OwnerID
    ConnectionID string
    Version      int        // 1, 2, ... one more per replacement or refresh
    Kind         string     // "api_token", "oauth_tokens", "app_installation"
    Ciphertext   []byte     // self-describing envelope from the Cryptographer
    ExpiresAt    *time.Time // for the access token, if known
    CreatedAt    time.Time
}

The plaintext structure for each Kind is private to its provider and sealed as a whole. The ciphertext is a self-describing envelope, so it records which key version sealed it and needs no separate key reference. Credentials are append-only by version, and the credential store tracks the active version. Older versions are kept until the connection's credentials are destroyed, so a replacement can be validated before it is activated.

docs.title: Grants and bindings
docs.text:
type Grant struct {
    Owner        OwnerID
    ConnectionID string
    Principal    Principal
    Actions      []Action // use, manage, share, disconnect
}

type Binding struct {
    Owner        OwnerID
    ConnectionID string
    Consumer     Consumer // kind and id: application, workflow, agent
    Purpose      string   // e.g. "code-health"
}

A grant is authority; a binding is dependency. Deleting a connection lists bindings first.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Every port method takes an Owner or a record that carries it, and an implementation must scope by it.

type ConnectionStore interface {
    CreateConnection(ctx context.Context, c Connection) (Connection, error) // revision 1; ErrExists
    GetConnection(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, id string) (Connection, error)
    ListConnections(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, f Filter) ([]Connection, error)
    // UpdateConnection replaces c iff the stored revision equals c.Revision,
    // else ErrConflict; a forbidden state change is ErrInvalidTransition.
    UpdateConnection(ctx context.Context, c Connection) (Connection, error)
    DeleteConnection(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, id string) error // cascades
}

type CredentialStore interface {
    // SwapCredential installs next as active iff the active version is
    // expectActive (0 for none) and next.Version == expectActive+1.
    SwapCredential(ctx context.Context, expectActive int, next Credential) error
    ActiveCredential(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, connID string) (Credential, error)
    DestroyCredentials(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, connID string) error
}

// GrantStore and BindingStore put, remove and list by connection.
// Store embeds all four, so one type can implement them.

type Cryptographer interface {
    Seal(ctx context.Context, purpose string, plaintext, aad []byte) ([]byte, error)
    Open(ctx context.Context, purpose string, ciphertext, aad []byte) ([]byte, error)
}

type Authorizer interface {
    Allowed(ctx context.Context, p Principal, a Action, conn Connection) error // ErrDenied
}

type Auditor interface {
    Record(ctx context.Context, e Event) error
}

type Leaser interface {
    // Acquire returns a lease or ErrLeaseHeld. The lease is released or expires.
    Acquire(ctx context.Context, key string, ttl time.Duration) (Lease, error)
}

type SecretSource interface {
    // Secret reads a deployment secret, such as an OAuth client secret or a
    // GitHub App private key, from the host's secret manager.
    Secret(ctx context.Context, ref string) (Secret, error)
}
  • Cryptographer binds aad to the owner, connection ID and credential version, so a ciphertext cannot be moved between connections or tenants. The purpose is connectionforge.credential. The port is deliberately the same shape as an envelope-encryption client's encrypt and decrypt, so a key-management library satisfies it with a small adapter in the host.
  • Leaser is how refresh is made single-flight across processes. A host may implement it with an advisory lock or a lease row; the in-memory implementation is for tests.
  • Authorizer is called by service and by the broker. A failed authorization is an error, never a silent downgrade.
  • Auditor returns an error. An operation whose event cannot be recorded reports it; it is never dropped silently.
  • SecretSource is how deployment secrets reach the library. A secret manager (for example omnivault) implements it in the host. Per-owner credentials never go through it: they are sealed and stored as above.

docs.title: The SQL store
docs.text:
sqlstore implements ConnectionStore, CredentialStore, the grant and binding stores and Leaser over Ent, for SQLite and PostgreSQL. The memory store remains the reference for behaviour, and both run the same conformance suite.

store, err := sqlstore.New(db, sqlstore.Postgres,
    sqlstore.WithTxHook(func(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx) error {
        return setTenant(ctx, tx) // host-supplied, e.g. SET LOCAL for RLS
    }))
err = store.Migrate(ctx)
tables := store.Tables() // for the host's tenancy policy
  • Own generated client. The Ent schema and generated code live in sqlstore/ent. The host does not regenerate or merge them into its own client; it shares the database, not the code generation.
  • Table names are prefixed connectionforge_, so they cannot collide with the host's.
  • Tenant column. Every table carries owner_id (text). Every query filters on it in code; a host that enables row-level security keys its policy on the same column, so isolation holds twice.
  • Every operation runs in a transaction and calls the host's TxHook first, so session variables such as a tenant setting apply to it. A hook error aborts the operation.
  • Uniqueness and swaps are in the database. Credential versions are unique per connection and the active version is the highest, so two concurrent SwapCredential calls for the same version are decided by the unique index. UpdateConnection is a conditional update on the revision, and its affected-row count decides the outcome.
  • The lease table has no owner. Lease names (for example refresh:<connection>) are not owned records, so Tables() leaves the lease table out of the host's tenancy policy.
  • No driver is imported. The host opens the database with the driver it already uses. A SQLite database needs foreign keys on (Ent requires it to migrate) and one connection or immediate transactions, so writers queue.
  • Leases are rows with an expiry, acquired by a conditional insert or update, so refresh is single-flight across processes with no other infrastructure.
  • The schema is versioned with the module. A change that alters stored data needs a migration note in the changelog.
  • Ciphertext is stored as bytes; no column ever holds plaintext.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
type Secret struct{ v []byte }

func (Secret) String() string               { return "[redacted]" }
func (Secret) GoString() string             { return "[redacted]" }
func (Secret) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(`"[redacted]"`), nil }
func (Secret) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte("[redacted]"), nil }
func (Secret) LogValue() slog.Value         { return slog.StringValue("[redacted]") }
func (s Secret) Reveal() []byte             { return s.v } // narrow, grep-able
  • Reveal is called only inside provider adapters and the broker. A test (boundary_test.go) fails on a call to Reveal anywhere else.
  • Errors from adapters are classified (ErrInvalidCredential, ErrInsufficientScope, ErrTransient, ErrRateLimited, ...) and carry the provider's status and request ID, never a request or response body that could echo a credential.
  • Plaintext buffers are zeroed after use on a best-effort basis.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
type Provider interface {
    Manifest() Manifest
    // Validate checks the credential with the provider, using an HTTP client
    // the caller restricted to the manifest's hosts, and returns the account.
    Validate(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m Material) (Result, error)
    // Authenticate adds the credential to the caller's copy of a request.
    Authenticate(r *http.Request, m Material) error
}

// Optional capabilities, discovered by type assertion (later phases).
type Refresher  interface { Refresh(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m Material) (Material, error) }
type Revoker    interface { Revoke(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m Material) error }
type Discoverer interface { Accounts(ctx context.Context, hc *http.Client, m Material) ([]Account, error) }

Material is the unsealed credential handed to an adapter inside the broker: a kind, its fields as Secret values, and an expiry. It is encoded for sealing by the provider package, versioned, with field values as bytes so they can be cleared. A provider never makes its own HTTP client; it uses the one it is given, so egress policy applies to validation as well as use. Adapters classify a refusal with provider.Classify: 401 and other 4xx are an invalid credential, 403 an insufficient scope, 429 rate limiting and 5xx transient; the error carries the status and the provider's request ID, never a body. Refresh and revoke are optional because static keys do not support them; the broker and the service check the capability and degrade explicitly (a non-refreshing connection that expires moves to needs_attention).

docs.title: Manifest
docs.text:
A manifest is data, so a UI can render a connection form and an agent can read what a connection needs:

{
  "key": "cloudflare",
  "displayName": "Cloudflare",
  "baseUrls": ["https://api.cloudflare.com"],
  "authMethods": [{
    "key": "api_token",
    "fields": [
      {"name": "token", "label": "API token", "secret": true, "required": true}
    ],
    "scopes": [{"name": "zone:read"}, {"name": "analytics:read"}],
    "accountSelection": "discovered",
    "validation": {"operation": "verify_token"},
    "helpUrl": "https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/"
  }]
}

Property names are camelCase (a document format owned here). A manifest never contains executable content. Secret fields are never echoed back by any API.

docs.title: Reference providers
docs.text:
Provider Method Validation Discovery Static token (driven by manifest) API key or token in a header A GET to a manifest-named verification endpoint; status classification Account and label from the response through a manifest path GitHub App App ID and private key held as host configuration; per-connection installation ID Mint an installation token, then read the installation Account login, repository selection, granted permissions

For GitHub App, the long-lived material is the app key, held by the host (through a SecretSource), not per-connection. The connection holds only the installation ID, so there is no stored long-lived credential per tenant. The broker mints installation tokens, caches them until a margin before expiry and records their permissions.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
• Authorization code with PKCE (S256) always, even for confidential clients. State is bound to owner, principal and a validated return destination, stored server-side with a short expiry and single use.
  • Return destinations are allow-listed by the host. A callback never redirects to a value taken from the request.
  • Scopes are the minimum the enabled features need; a reconnect that adds a scope is a distinct consent.
  • Callbacks are handled by the library (or httpapi), never by an embedded application.
  • Token exchange uses golang.org/x/oauth2; the library does not implement the protocol.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text:
1. The broker finds the access token expired or within the margin.
  2. It acquires a lease on refresh:<connection> from the Leaser. If the lease is held, it waits and re-reads the credential; one exchange is enough for all callers.
  3. It reads the active credential, calls the adapter's Refresh, seals the result and installs it with Swap(expectVersion). A rotated refresh token is part of the new sealed material, so access and refresh token change atomically.
  4. Failure classification: invalid_grant or revocation moves the connection to needs_attention; network, 5xx and rate-limit responses set health and retry with backoff, leaving state unchanged.

If the exchange succeeds but Swap fails (a concurrent writer), the new tokens are discarded and the winner's credential is used; with providers that rotate refresh tokens on use, the loser re-reads before ever calling the provider.

docs.title: Broker
docs.text:
type Broker interface {
    // HTTPClient returns a client whose requests are authenticated for the
    // connection. It never exposes the credential.
    HTTPClient(ctx context.Context, owner OwnerID, p Principal, connID string, use Use) (*http.Client, error)
}
  • Authorization (use) and state are checked each time a client is made, and the Use (consumer and purpose) is reported to an optional OnUse hook for counters, not recorded as an event per request. A refusal is audited.
  • The credential is unsealed once, when the client is made, and the transport adds it to a copy of each request. A caller makes a client per unit of work, so a disconnect or a replaced credential applies to the next client. Refresh (phase 3) happens when a client is made, under the lease.
  • The client is wrapped by egress: a request whose host is not in the provider's manifest baseUrls is refused, redirects to another host are refused, and resolved private, loopback and link-local addresses are refused unless the host explicitly allows a development destination.
  • The result is an *http.Client a provider SDK can accept (WithHTTPClient), which is how SDKs consume a connection without connectionforge importing them.

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
service runs the operations a host exposes. Each authorizes through the host's Authorizer, audits, and retries a lost compare-and-swap a bounded number of times.

Operation Action Behaviour Create manage Checks fields against the manifest, validates with the provider, and stores the connection and its sealed credential only if the provider accepts it Get, List view List returns only the connections the actor may view Rename manage Changes the display name Test use Validates again; the outcome goes to health. A permanent failure moves the connection to needs_attention, success back to connected, a transient failure changes only health Disconnect disconnect Marks it disconnected and destroys its credentials; the record stays

An audit failure after a successful change returns ErrNotAudited: the change was made and the gap in the trail is reported, not hidden.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: Events: connection.created, connection.validated, connection.state_changed, credential.replaced, credential.refreshed, credential.revoked, connection.used (counters), connection.shared, connection.disconnected, grant.changed, access.denied, admin.read. Each carries owner, actor (principal and, where applicable, on-behalf-of principal), connection ID, provider and outcome. No event carries a secret or a response body.

docs.title: Delegated authorization (design only)
docs.text:
The model leaves room without implementing it:

  • Principal distinguishes a user, a service and an agent, and a use may carry an OnBehalfOf principal and an evidence reference.
  • AuthMethod is an open string. A future method (workload identity, token exchange, DPoP-bound tokens, an agent-authorization flow) is a provider whose Authenticate obtains authorization per request and stores no long-lived secret; the connection record is unchanged.
  • The Authorizer receives the principal, the action, the connection and the use, so policy can bind access to an operation, not only to a connection.

docs.title: Threat model (summary)
docs.text:
Threat Mitigation Stolen database contents Credentials are ciphertext under a managed key; AAD binds to owner and connection Cross-tenant access Owner is in every port signature; conformance suite proves refusal Secret in logs, errors, responses Secret type, classified errors, no bodies in errors, Reveal lint SSRF through a configurable endpoint Endpoints come from the manifest; egress policy; no user-supplied base URL except by host allow-list Open redirect or callback hijack Server-side single-use state, PKCE, allow-listed return destinations Lost refresh token under concurrency Lease plus compare-and-swap; rotated token persisted atomically Compromised app private key (GitHub App) Held by the host through a secret source; short-lived installation tokens; documented rotation Confused deputy through a shared connection Grants checked per use; bindings record purpose; audit of each use class

Known limitations are recorded in this section as they are found.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Store conformance suite (storetest): tenancy isolation, compare-and- swap, active-version swap, destroy, listing filters. Every store, including the host's, runs it.
  • Cryptographer conformance: round trip, AAD mismatch fails, wrong purpose fails, no plaintext in the stored value.
  • Provider fixtures: recorded HTTP responses with httptest, covering valid, revoked, insufficient scope, rate-limited and provider-error cases. Fixtures contain no real tokens.
  • Concurrency: N goroutines refreshing one connection produce one exchange and a consistent final credential; race detector clean.
  • Leak tests: every error and event type is asserted not to contain a sentinel secret placed in the credential.
  • Egress tests: redirects, DNS rebinding to a private address and off-manifest hosts are refused.
  • Integration tests against live providers are opt-in by environment variable and excluded from the default run.
